Riders in the Croatian capital of Zagreb are now able to order a Pony.ai robotaxi on the Uber platform.

The move is part of an agreement between Pony.ai and Uber Technologies to deploy more than 2,000 Pony.ai robotaxis across Europe.

Pony.ai operates paid, fully-driverless services in four Chinese cities.

The plan is to add services in four other cities in Europe, with deployment in the Middle East also on the roadmap.

Uber has been active in the autonomous vehicle space, signing an agreement this year with automaker Stellantis, AI company Wayve.

It also plans with WeRide to jointly launch Spain’s first commercial robotaxi pilot.

Three core functions

Pony.ai says three core functions are required to operate robotaxi services at scale:

Level 4 (L4) autonomous driving technology

A mobility platform

Day-to-day fleet operations.

It allows technology, platform and fleet partners to work together in the same market, while individual partners may also take on more than one role.

Vehicle funding and ownership can sit with different partners, depending on the market.

For the new partnership, Pony.ai will provide its L4 autonomous driving technology, rider experience and operational expertise.

Uber will provide customer access through its global mobility platform, including booking, payment and customer service capabilities.

Day-to-day fleet operations may be carried out by established local fleet partners selected for each market.

Zagreb service

For example, the new Zagreb service is operated by local provider Verne.

Riders will be able to access robotaxis in the city – including the city centre – from 7am to 9pm, with the service set to expand over time.

At this stage, a human operator will also be on board, monitoring behind the wheel, before fully-driverless operations begin in the future, Pony.ai says.

The company was founded in China in 2016 and began collaborating with Uber in May 2025.

“This expanded agreement marks an important new phase in the partnership between Pony.ai and Uber,” said James Peng, founder and CEO of Pony.ai.

“It reflects our shared commitment to bringing safe, reliable robotaxi services to more European cities.”

Sarfraz Maredia, global head of autonomous mobility and delivery at Uber, says: “The next chapter for autonomous mobility is about moving from individual launches to repeatable commercial scale.”

“Together with Pony.ai, we’re combining advanced autonomous technology with Uber’s hybrid platform, on-the-ground experience and operational excellence to build a model that can quickly and reliably expand across cities.”

title: Walmart sees slowest pace in US comparable sales in 6 years, offers cautious guidance
description:
Comparable sales in U.S. stores, which measure sales at stores open at least a year along with online sales tied to those locations, rose 2.6% in the second quarter.
Some of the slowing growth was related to how pharmacies are regulated in the U.S., including those in Walmart stores.
Excluding the wellness category that includes Walmart’s pharmacies, comparable sales increased 3.4% in the second quarter.
For the third quarter, Walmart expects earnings per share of 62 cents to 64 cents.
The forecasts are below analysts’ expectations of 68 cents per share and sales of $188.19 billion, according to FactSet.
text:
NEW YORK -- Walmart experienced the slowest growth in comparable sales at U.S. stores in six years in its most recent quarter and it offered a cautious outlook for the year, sending shares down 6% before the opening bell Thursday.

Comparable sales in U.S. stores, which measure sales at stores open at least a year along with online sales tied to those locations, rose 2.6% in the second quarter. They rose 4.1% in the previous quarter.

Some of the slowing growth was related to how pharmacies are regulated in the U.S., including those in Walmart stores. Federal legislations require pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.

Excluding the wellness category that includes Walmart’s pharmacies, comparable sales increased 3.4% in the second quarter. However, even accounting for regulations, the sales were still below industry analyst expectations for a 3.8% increase, according to FactSet.

Walmart’s U.S. e-commerce business, which has become an engine of growth for the retailer, rose 24%, trailing the first-quarter pace of 26%.

Walmart is among the first batch of major retailers to report second-quarter results, which could offer industry analysts and economists another read on whether ongoing price pressures from the conflict in Iran have impacted consumer behavior.

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers are on its website or in its stores every week, according to Walmart.

That may draw even more attention this quarter after U.S. data released Friday showed that retail sales were surprisingly weak in July and a new read on consumers from the University of Michigan revealed growing pessimism about the economy, with so many Americans struggling with higher costs for gas, groceries and just about everything else.

The new figures from Walmart revealed the smallest gain in comparable store sales since a 1.9% gain for the quarter ended Jan. 31, 2020, according to FactSet.

That has broadened Walmart’s customer base and the retailer has begun capturing a larger share of wealthier Americans. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart are coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $6.37 billion, or 80 cents per share, in the three-month period ended July 31. Adjusted per-share results were 81 cents, easily topping the 74 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet.

Sales rose 5.9% to $187.94 billion. Analysts were predicting $186.62 billion, according to FactSet.

For the third quarter, Walmart expects earnings per share of 62 cents to 64 cents. It projects sales to be up 3% to 3.5%. That would put sales in a range of $184.88 billion to $186.23 billion. The forecasts are below analysts’ expectations of 68 cents per share and sales of $188.19 billion, according to FactSet.

For the full year, Walmart now expects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.80 to $2.87 while sales should be up anywhere from 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $741.7 billion to $748.8 billion, according to FactSet.

Analysts expected $2.90 per share and sales of $752.06 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

text:
Riders in Zagreb become the first in Europe to book an AV through Uber, powered by Pony.ai and operated by Verne.

ZAGREB, Croatia, August 19, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Uber Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: UBER), Verne and Pony AI Inc. ("Pony.ai") (NASDAQ: PONY; HKEX: 2026) today announced the launch of autonomous rides on the Uber app in Zagreb, marking the first time riders in Europe can book an AV with Uber.

From today, riders can book an autonomous ride within key areas of Zagreb, including the city centre, with service availability and geographic coverage set to expand over time. At launch, a licensed operator will be on-board monitoring behind the wheel, as part of our phased introduction, before fully driverless operations begin in the future.

The new service brings together Pony.ai's autonomous driving technology, Verne's service ecosystem and operational framework, and Uber's global mobility platform. Under this model, Pony.ai provides its autonomous driving solution; Verne acts as fleet owner and service operator; and Uber integrates the service into its ride-hailing network and delivers the rider experience via its app.

The launch builds on the partnership announced in March, moving the service from development and testing to real-world deployment on Uber.

"Today marks a major milestone for autonomous mobility in Europe," said Annie Duvnjak, Global Head of Autonomous Mobility Operations at Uber. "By bringing together Pony.ai's proven autonomous-driving technology, Verne's operational expertise and Uber's global platform, we're making it simple for riders to access autonomous rides through the Uber app. Zagreb is an important first step as we work to bring AVs to millions of riders and build the world's largest platform for AV deployment."

Zagreb is the first market to launch under the partnership and provides a model that the companies plan to scale to additional European cities. Further details on the next markets to launch will be announced later this year.

"Verne launched Europe's first commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb in April. Since then, we have completed thousands of autonomous rides, operating every day and learning from real customers in a real European city. From today, Verne rides are also available through Uber, giving customers another way to access the service. This marks another European first — the first time autonomous rides are available through Uber in Europe," said Marko Pejkovic, CEO of Verne, "This is an important milestone not only for Verne, but also for Croatia. A service pioneered here in Zagreb is now available through the world's largest mobility platform. The experience we are gaining every day in Zagreb will help us bring Verne to other European cities."

text:
K-beauty is booming in Australia. But as Korean skincare continues to capture Australian consumers and retail shelf space, one homegrown beauty brand is reversing the flow, expanding into South Korea itself.

Australia’s appetite for Korean beauty shows little sign of slowing. Once a relatively niche corner of the beauty market, K-beauty has moved firmly into the Australian mainstream, spanning specialist retailers, pharmacies, department stores and major beauty destinations.

The numbers tell the story. As previously reported by Retail Beauty, according to Future Market Insights, Australians are now the biggest global spenders per capita on South Korean beauty products outside Korea itself, fuelled by social media, K-pop celebrity influence and the reputation of K-beauty formulations for innovation and efficacy.

And the growth has been rapid. In 2024, South Korea accounted for 10.8 per cent of Australian imports across the HS 3304 cosmetics category, with imports from Korea increasing 32.8 per cent year-on-year.

But while Korean brands are increasingly looking to Australia for growth, one Australian skincare company is making the journey in reverse.

Australian beauty heads to Korea

Australian skincare and wellness brand Sasy n Savy has expanded its South Korean retail presence, launching into Galleria Department Store Gwanggyo and AK Department Store Bundang earlier this month.

Founded in Australia in 2000 by Samea Maakrun, Sasy n Savy offers skincare, body care, hair care, sun protection and wellness products, with its formulations combining Australian botanical ingredients with a vegan and organic-led brand positioning.

For an Australian brand, entering South Korea represents an interesting proposition. Korea isn’t simply another international beauty market; it is one of the industry’s most influential centres for formulation, product innovation, manufacturing and emerging skincare trends.

“Korea is recognised globally for its sophisticated beauty consumers and strong appreciation for quality skincare. To have Sasy n Savy available through leading department stores such as Galleria and AK is an important step in our international growth,” Maakrun said.

Reversing the K-Beauty flow

The significance of the expansion becomes clearer when viewed against the considerable imbalance in beauty trade between the two countries.

In 2025, Australian imports of South Korean beauty and skincare preparations reached US$180.07 million in 2025, according to UN Comtrade data. Australian exports in the same category heading to South Korea totalled just US$8.71 million. That makes Sasy n Savy’s expansion notable beyond the addition of two new retail doors.

While Australian consumers increasingly look to Korea for beauty innovation, the brand is betting there is also an opportunity for Australian beauty propositions — particularly those built around Australian botanicals and wellness — within the highly competitive Korean market.

The company says South Korea forms part of a broader international growth strategy rather than representing a standalone retail expansion.

“Our goal is to build Sasy n Savy into an internationally recognised Australian skincare brand,” Maakrun said. “Entering the Korean market allows us to introduce our products to a new audience while continuing to grow our brand internationally.”

From K-Beauty to A-Beauty?

The expansion also raises a broader question for Australia’s beauty industry. Korean brands have demonstrated how a distinct national beauty identity can become an international commercial proposition. Australia’s own combination of botanical ingredients, wellness heritage, natural beauty positioning and established skincare expertise offers local brands a potentially differentiated story abroad.

For Sasy n Savy, entering one of the world’s most sophisticated and competitive skincare markets will put that proposition to the test.

At a time when Australia can’t seem to get enough of K-beauty, this Australian brand is betting Korean consumers might be ready for a little more A-beauty in return.
